title: Normal pregnancy: decreased systemic vascular resistance
vignette: A 38-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, at 34 weeks gestation comes to the office due to increasing swelling in her hands and legs. The patient first noticed the swelling a few weeks ago but now cannot stand for more than an hour without needing to elevate her legs. She has no orthopnea, dyspnea, or chest pain. The patient has no chronic medical conditions and takes no daily medications. Vital signs are normal. Cardiac examination is within normal limits. Lungs are clear to auscultation. Bilateral lower extremities have 2+ pitting edema to the midshin. Urine dipstick shows no protein. Compared to a healthy nonpregnant woman, which of the following parameters is most likely to be decreased in this patient?

clues.note: Third-trimester pregnancy involves major cardiovascular adaptations - increased cardiac output/plasma volume and decreased systemic vascular resistance.
Dependent lower-extremity edema is common in normal pregnancy (increased plasma volume + decreased plasma oncotic pressure + venous compression), not necessarily pathologic.
No proteinuria (and normal BP) argues against preeclampsia - this is physiologic pregnancy edema.

whatMatters: Normal pregnancy markedly DECREASES SYSTEMIC VASCULAR RESISTANCE (via vasodilators like nitric oxide/progesterone and the low-resistance uteroplacental circuit). This is the dominant hemodynamic change; it triggers RAAS activation and volume expansion, so plasma volume, preload, and cardiac output all INCREASE. The parameter that DECREASES is SVR. Answer E.
strategy: Recall the pregnancy hemodynamic profile: DOWN = systemic vascular resistance (and blood pressure, especially mid-pregnancy) and pulmonary vascular resistance; UP = plasma volume (~40%), preload, stroke volume, cardiac output, and heart rate; central venous pressure stays roughly normal. The question asks what DECREASES -> SVR. Reject preload, cardiac output, plasma volume (all increased) and central venous pressure (unchanged).

eliminations.label: Cardiac preload - increased in pregnancy
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: ventricular end-diastolic volume/venous return. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: expanded plasma volume raises venous return and preload; it increases, not decreases. ✅ Correct if: asking what INCREASES with volume expansion.

eliminations.label: Cardiac output - increased ~30-50%
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: heart rate x stroke volume. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: cardiac output rises markedly (higher stroke volume + heart rate) to perfuse the uteroplacental unit. ✅ Correct if: asking what increases in pregnancy.

eliminations.label: Central venous pressure - roughly unchanged
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: right atrial filling pressure. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: increased venous capacitance and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance accommodate the extra volume, so CVP stays about NORMAL - it isn't the decreased parameter. ✅ Correct if: asking what stays unchanged.

eliminations.label: Plasma volume - increased up to ~40%
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: circulating plasma volume. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: RAAS activation from lower SVR expands plasma volume by up to 40% (physiologic anemia of pregnancy). ✅ Correct if: asking what increases (dilutional anemia).

reasoning: Pregnancy triggers widespread vasodilation and a low-resistance uteroplacental circuit
This markedly DECREASES systemic vascular resistance (the dominant change)
Lower SVR -> RAAS activation -> increased plasma volume, preload, and cardiac output
-> systemic vascular resistance is decreased; answer E
mechanism: During pregnancy the maternal cardiovascular system adapts to increase cardiac output and optimize fetal perfusion. The dominant hemodynamic change is a marked DECREASE in SYSTEMIC VASCULAR RESISTANCE (SVR), driven by increased vasodilators (nitric oxide, prostacyclin, progesterone), reduced vascular sensitivity to vasoconstrictors, and the creation of a high-flow, low-resistance uteroplacental circuit. The fall in SVR (and blood pressure, which dips in the second trimester) activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, causing fluid retention and a rise in PLASMA VOLUME of up to ~40%; this increases venous return (PRELOAD), and together with reduced afterload it boosts STROKE VOLUME and CARDIAC OUTPUT (heart rate also rises). Pulmonary vascular resistance decreases and venous capacitance increases, so CENTRAL VENOUS PRESSURE stays roughly normal despite the added volume. Peripheral edema is common (increased volume + reduced plasma oncotic pressure) even without preeclampsia. Therefore, compared with a nonpregnant woman, the DECREASED parameter is systemic vascular resistance.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Repro/Physio > pregnancy: ↓SVR, ↓PVR, ↓BP (mid-pregnancy); ↑plasma volume (~40%), ↑preload, ↑stroke volume, ↑cardiac output, ↑heart rate; CVP ~unchanged; physiologic anemia + edema.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: The dominant hemodynamic change is decreased SVR; most other parameters increase.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on systemic vascular resistance, preload, cardiac output, central venous pressure, or RAAS activation? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Preload, cardiac output, and plasma volume INCREASE; CVP is roughly unchanged - only SVR decreases.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: pregnancy = ↓SVR (dominant), ↑plasma volume/CO/preload, CVP unchanged; physiologic anemia + dependent edema.

firstAid.detail: Repro > preload/CO/plasma volume up; SVR/PVR/BP down.
OB > dependent edema common; no proteinuria/hypertension = not preeclampsia.

memoryHook: Pregnancy opens the vascular floodgates: resistance drops (↓SVR), so the body pours in extra volume and pumps more - the one thing going DOWN is SVR.
